temperature, different time: thickness decides how long the heat takes to reach the middle. Size Air fryer Oven Shoestring, ¼ inch (6 mm) 380°F / 195°C · 14 min 400°F / 205°C · 20 min Standard, ⅜ inch (1 cm) 380°F / 195°C · 18 min 400°F / 205°C · 26 min Steak fries, ½ inch (1.3 cm) and over 380°F / 195°C · 22 min 400°F / 205°C · 31 min Why fresh fries go limp or burn Fresh potatoes are full of water and surface starch. Put cut fries straight into the basket and the starch on the outside browns and catches while the inside is still raw, or the water steams them limp if the basket is crowded. Frozen fries avoid both problems because the factory has already blanched and dried them, which is why the frozen setting is different. At home, a soak does the same job: it rinses off loose starch, so the outside browns evenly instead of scorching in patches. Drying afterwards matters just as much. A wet fry spends its first minutes steaming, and a fry that has steamed never fully crisps. Worked example Two medium russets cut into ⅜-inch sticks, soaked in cold water for 30 minutes, dried thoroughly and tossed with a tablespoon of oil and salt. Cook in a single layer at 380°F for 18 minutes, shaking the basket twice. Shoestring fries need about 14 minutes and thick steak fries about 22. The oven version, on a tray at 400°F, takes around 26 minutes. How to tell they are done Look for an even golden colour with slightly darker edges, and listen: a done fry sounds hollow and crisp when it hits the others. Take one out and break it; the inside should be soft and floury, not translucent. If the outside is brown but the inside is still firm, the fries were cut too thick for the time, so give them three more minutes and lower the heat slightly next time. Before they go in Use floury potatoes such as russets or Maris Pipers. Cut the fries to an even thickness so they finish together; uneven batches always have burnt thin pieces and raw thick ones. Soak in cold water for at least 30 minutes, then dry them completely with a clean towel. A tablespoon of oil per two potatoes is enough. Salt after cooking, not before, or the salt draws out water. About 18 minutes at 380°F for standard ⅜-inch fries, shaken twice. Shoestring fries take around 14 minutes and steak fries around 22. Do I need to soak potatoes before air frying? It helps a lot. A 30-minute soak in cold water removes surface starch, so the fries brown evenly and crisp instead of scorching in patches. Why are my air fryer fries soggy? Usually they were still wet or the basket was too full. Dry them thoroughly and cook in a single layer, in batches if needed. Is this setting right for frozen fries? No. Frozen fries are already blanched and follow different rules; use frozen mode with the temperature from the bag. What is the oven equivalent for homemade fries? 400°F for around 26 minutes on a tray in a conventional oven, or 375°F for 20 minutes in a fan oven. mainEntity.name: How long do homemade fries take in the air fryer?

acceptedAnswer.text: About 18 minutes at 380°F for standard ⅜-inch fries, shaken twice. Shoestring fries take around 14 minutes and steak fries around 22.

mainEntity.name: Do I need to soak potatoes before air frying?

acceptedAnswer.text: It helps a lot. A 30-minute soak in cold water removes surface starch, so the fries brown evenly and crisp instead of scorching in patches.

mainEntity.name: Why are my air fryer fries soggy?

acceptedAnswer.text: Usually they were still wet or the basket was too full. Dry them thoroughly and cook in a single layer, in batches if needed.

mainEntity.name: Is this setting right for frozen fries?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. Frozen fries are already blanched and follow different rules; use frozen mode with the temperature from the bag.

mainEntity.name: What is the oven equivalent for homemade fries?

acceptedAnswer.text: 400°F for around 26 minutes on a tray in a conventional oven, or 375°F for 20 minutes in a fan oven.
